_why: A pre-push hook is the guard shape with the weakest natural feedback: on a clean tree a correct hook and a hook that unconditionally exits 0 are byte-identical, and nobody notices the difference until the drift it was installed to catch is already on main. So every mutation here forces the hook toward exit 0 or toward sweeping nothing -- the two ways it dies quietly -- and each is pinned to the test that must bite. The installer mutations cover the other half: an install that reports success while linking nothing, linking into the wrong repository, or destroying somebody else's hook.

mutations.name: drift-allows-the-push
mutations._mechanism: The whole point, deleted. The hook still runs, still prints, still reports the drift -- and the push succeeds. A reviewer reading the output sees the block message and would not notice.

mutations.name: nothing-swept-reads-as-clean
mutations._mechanism: Collapse ANCHORS_NOTHING_SWEPT into the ANCHORS_OK arm. Nothing was measured, and the hook says nothing at all -- the exact 'a null reads as absence' failure the sweep exists to prevent, now silent at the push boundary.

mutations.name: broken-tooling-blocks-every-push
mutations._mechanism: The inverse failure, and the one that makes an operator uninstall the guard. A harness that crashed measured nothing; treating that as drift blocks every push in the clone until someone repairs unrelated tooling.
mutations.find:
printf 'Treating as broken tooling, not as drift. Push ALLOWED.\n' >&2
        exit 0
mutations.replace:
printf 'Treating as broken tooling, not as drift. Push ALLOWED.\n' >&2
        exit 1

mutations.name: missing-harness-blocks-every-push
mutations._mechanism: Same failure one step earlier: the harness is simply not installed, which is the normal state of a clone that has never run h-mad. Blocking there makes the hook hostile to every repo it is installed in by default.

mutations.name: discovery-sweeps-nothing
mutations._mechanism: Break discovery and the hook exits 0 on the empty-candidates path -- silently, from every repository. This is the mutation a hardcoded spec directory would have made permanent: the sweep is over what git tracks, and if that list comes back empty the guard is decoration.

mutations.name: override-is-ignored
mutations._mechanism: HMAD_MUTATION_SPEC_DIR silently falls through to discovery. The operator set it precisely because discovery is wrong for their repo, and the hook reports a verdict over the wrong set of specs.

mutations.name: override-widens-instead-of-replacing
mutations._mechanism: Let discovery run alongside the override. An override that can only ADD specs cannot exclude one, so the operator has no way to narrow a sweep that is blocking their pushes for a spec they do not own.
mutations.replace:
CANDIDATES=$(printf '%s\n%s' "$CANDIDATES" "$(git -c core.quotePath=false ls-files -- '*.json' 2>/dev/null || true)" | grep -v '^$' || true)
if false; then

mutations.name: empty-candidates-still-invokes-the-harness
mutations._mechanism: Drop the early exit and a repo with no JSON at all reaches --check-anchors with zero arguments: argparse refuses, no ANCHORS_* token is printed, and every push in every specless repository prints a tooling warning. Noise on a path that has nothing to say trains the operator to ignore the one that does.

mutations.name: installer-destroys-a-foreign-hook
mutations._mechanism: Back up nothing. Somebody else's pre-push is deleted by an installer whose output says 'installed' -- unrecoverable, and invisible until the hook they wrote stops firing.

mutations.name: uninstall-removes-someone-elses-hook
mutations._mechanism: The ownership test is what makes --uninstall safe to run blind. Without it the flag deletes whatever sits at that path, which is the one thing an uninstaller must never do.

mutations.name: installs-under-a-set-core-hookspath
mutations._mechanism: Git reads hooks from core.hooksPath, so the link lands somewhere git will never look. The installer reports success, the smoke test passes, and the guard never runs once -- a guard that cannot fire is worse than no guard, because it is believed.

mutations.name: installer-smoke-test-never-fails
mutations._mechanism: The smoke test exists so a hook that would block every push is reported at install time rather than discovered on the next push. Silence it and the operator learns about it from a failed push, mid-task.
mutations.find: echo "WARNING: $hook exited non-zero on the current tree — it will block pushes." >&2

mutations.name: installer-copies-instead-of-linking
mutations._mechanism: A copy is the failure h_mad_install_check.py was written for, one level down: it keeps working while drifting arbitrarily far from the checkout, and nothing downstream can tell the two apart.

mutations.name: installs-outside-a-git-repository
mutations._mechanism: Without the check, `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` in a non-repo directory walks UP to any enclosing repository and installs there. Running the installer in a scratch directory then silently arms a hook in the parent clone.

mutations.name: an-unreadable-target-stops-blocking
mutations._mechanism: The J37 coupling, restored. Drop ANCHORS_UNREADABLE from the blocking arm and a spec whose target file is GONE falls through to the catch-all: the push is allowed, and the harness's real verdict is reported to the operator as 'no ANCHORS_* verdict ... broken tooling'. Measured live during the J37 fix -- this is not hypothetical, it is what the hook did the moment the harness gained the new word.

_why_not_absolute_path_format: An `installer-links-into-the-callers-repo` mutation was written and REMOVED as equivalent, recorded here so a later reader does not re-add it. Dropping `--path-format=absolute` from the `--git-common-dir` call survives every test, and measurement says it should: the relative form git returns is relative to the CWD ('.git' from the top level, '../../.git' from a subdirectory, already absolute from a linked worktree), and the installer resolves it AFTER its only `cd` and never changes directory again -- so both forms name the same directory. The failure the flag guards against is the `-C <other-repo> rev-parse --git-common-dir` shape, which resolves '.git' against the CALLER's cwd and silently answers about the wrong repository; this script uses `cd`, not `-C`. The flag stays because it keeps the operator-facing paths absolute and survives a future edit that adds a `cd`, but it is defence in depth, not a live guard, and a mutant of it is indistinguishable from a real coverage gap. The properties it was reaching for are pinned directly by TestInstaller::test_installs_from_a_subdirectory_of_the_repo and ::test_installs_from_a_linked_worktree_into_the_common_dir.
